Chapter 15 brings the gods' own flawed relationships into view and shows how Riordan borrows a story from Homer's Odyssey.","enduringUnderstanding":"Myths are retold across time, and each retelling can keep the same human themes, such as jealousy, betrayal, and trickery, while changing voice, tone, and detail to speak to a new audience.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 23, students plan and draft their own archetype-based modern retellings. Today's analysis of how Riordan modernizes a myth gives them a model for choosing voice, tone, and detail.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students compare themes across versions of a mythic relationship. What stayed the same?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"When someone retells a story for a new audience, what do they usually keep, and what do they change?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They keep the main idea and the characters' problems, like in a remake of a fairy tale. But they change the setting, how people talk, and sometimes make it funnier or more modern."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today we meet a very old story about gods who feel jealous and get tricked. Homer's poem tells it one way. Riordan hints at it in Chapter 15 in another. We will compare the two and decide what each version makes us think about the gods."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to about three minutes of talk. Watch me with *crippled* on p. 232. In this chapter it describes the god Hephaestus and also machinery. I ask, does it mean injured, or broken and unable to work? Both fit, so I know the word can describe people or things that cannot function well."},{"type":"directions","text":"Open your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer. With a partner, find each word on its page and use the sentence to guess a meaning: brutal (p. 225), sneer (p. 226), proposition (p. 226), suspicions (p. 228), clouded (p. 229). Then do the same for temperamental (p. 230), defunct (p. 231), gossip (p. 232), crippled (p. 232), and marooned (p. 233). Write a meaning in your own words, a clue from the text, and a quick sketch or synonym."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"On p. 229, the text says something *clouded* a character's thinking. Can a thought really be covered by clouds? What does clouded mean here?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It is not real clouds. Clouded means his thinking was not clear because strong feelings got in the way, like when clouds make it hard to see the sky."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"*Temperamental* contains the word *temper*. How does that help you work out what it means for a god or a machine to be temperamental?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Temper means mood or anger, so temperamental means someone or something that changes moods fast or blows up easily. A temperamental machine would work one minute and quit the next."},{"type":"directions","text":"Review: Choose three words from this week's vocabulary, including at least two from today. Write one sentence for each that shows you know the meaning. Trade with a partner and check each other's work."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Spend about five minutes on the context work and five on the organizer and review. If students have words from earlier this week, let them choose from the organizer. Collect nothing; circulate and spot-check sentences."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in using context and word parts to determine meanings and in building precise vocabulary for describing characters and settings.","sayAsk":"Have students say each word aloud with a partner. Prompt: What clue in the sentence helped you? Frames: I think ___ means ___ because the sentence says ___. This word is similar to ___ in my home language. The word ___ can mean ___ or ___, but here it means ___. Encourage students to expand noun phrases, such as a brutal, rocky tunnel.","watchFor":"If students copy a dictionary definition without checking it against the sentence, then prompt: Does that meaning fit here? If students pick only one meaning for crippled or clouded, then prompt: Does this word have another meaning? Reread with a pencil. Mark the dialogue among Percy, Annabeth, and Ares about the ride and Hephaestus's traps, mark anything about Aphrodite's behavior, and circle similes, hyperbole, and other figurative language."},{"type":"directions","text":"Make a two-column chart. Left column: a quote or detail from pp. 224–233, such as dialogue, a trap, or Aphrodite's behavior. Right column: what it shows about the gods' relationships or the tone. Include at least two examples of figurative language."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Find a simile or hyperbole in the Tunnel of Love setting or in Ares's dramatic speech. What does it mean, and what does it do for the tone?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Ares's speech is full of exaggeration, like he is acting like the biggest tragedy ever happened to him. The hyperbole makes the god of war sound dramatic and a little silly instead of scary, so the tone is funny."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do the dialogue and Hephaestus's traps tell us about how these gods treat each other?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They show jealousy and tricks. Hephaestus set traps because he was upset about Ares and Aphrodite, and Ares talks like he is the victim, so the gods are not noble. They hold grudges and act petty, just like people."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.4","L.6.5.a"],"stem":"What is the main effect of the exaggerated language in the Tunnel of Love setting and Ares's dramatic speech in Chapter 15?","choices":[{"text":"It makes the scene humorous and a little silly, so the gods seem less grand and more like people.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. The exaggeration pokes fun at the gods, creating a humorous, modern tone that shows their very human flaws."},{"text":"It makes the setting seem calm and romantic so readers trust the gods.","correct":false,"rationale":"Students may be misled by the name Tunnel of Love. The figurative language is funny, not sincerely romantic."},{"text":"It shows that the gods are serious and powerful and should be feared.","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses dramatic with scary. The overblown speech undercuts the gods' dignity."},{"text":"It gives facts about how Hephaestus built the traps.","correct":false,"rationale":"Figurative language creates tone and meaning rather than technical information."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading closely, interpreting figurative language, and explaining effects on tone with precise noun phrases.","sayAsk":"Say: Find words that mean one thing literally but something else here. Ask: What is being compared? How does it make the scene feel? Frames: The author compares ___ to ___, which shows ___. The exaggeration makes the tone ___. Encourage expanded noun phrases: Ares's dramatic, over-the-top speech.","watchFor":"If students take figurative language literally, then prompt: Could this really happen? What feeling is the author creating? If students list quotes without explaining, then prompt: What does this detail show about the gods? Success: students name the comparison or exaggeration and its effect on tone."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: spotting and interpreting figurative language","tryThis":"Point to one example and ask What two things are compared? Is this literally true? Then have students restate it in plain words before naming the effect."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: effect on tone and meaning","tryThis":"Ask students to rewrite one figurative line in plain language and explain what tone is lost, then say which version better fits a funny retelling."}]}]},{"id":"lia-read-homer","title":"Part B1: Read the Homeric Excerpt","minutes":8,"standards":["RL.6.9","RL.6.1","RL.6.6"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Song of Ares and Aphrodite (adapted excerpt from Homer's Odyssey, Book 8)"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Now we read the older version. In Homer's poem, a singer tells how Hephaestus traps Aphrodite and Ares in a net and the gods look on and comment. Read with the same pencil: mark the narrator's voice, how the gods talk about the pair, and the level of detail."},{"type":"directions","text":"Read the excerpt. Add a third column to your chart or start a new Venn diagram labeled Homer, Both, Riordan. Record at least two details about Homer's version: who is betrayed, how Hephaestus tricks them, how the gods react."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In Homer's poem, how do the other gods react once the lovers are caught?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They gather and comment on the scene, and some laugh and make remarks about Ares and Aphrodite's behavior. It is told in a formal, poetic way, like a song, with more detail about the net and what the gods say."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How is the narrator's voice here different from the narrator's voice in Chapter 15?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Homer's voice is formal and serious, like a bard telling a story to an audience. Percy's voice in Riordan is casual, funny, and speaks in modern language."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"The excerpt is adapted. If students are unsure which myth Riordan refers to, point to the Tunnel of Love, Hephaestus's traps, and Aphrodite and Ares's relationship as the shared elements."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading closely across two texts and expressing similarities and differences using precise language.","sayAsk":"Say: Read one sentence at a time with a partner and retell it. Ask: Who is tricked? Who watches? Frames: In Homer's version, ___. In Riordan's version, ___. Both versions show ___. Allow students to discuss in a home language first, then restate in English.","watchFor":"If students retell the plot without comparing, then prompt: What is the same and what is different? If students confuse the gods' names, then provide a name list. Success: students record a detail from each version in correct columns."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: reading the older, formal text","tryThis":"Chunk the excerpt into short parts and have students write a one-line summary beside each, using who, what, and why."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: narrator and point of view","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how the singer's point of view shapes what we think of Ares and Aphrodite, and how Riordan's narrator changes that view."}]}]},{"id":"lia-compare-write","title":"Part B2: Compare the Versions and Write","minutes":12,"standards":["RL.6.9","L.6.6","RL.6.6"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teach","move":"teach","text":"A comparison paragraph names the shared theme, then shows how each text handles it. Use signal words such as *both*, *however*, and *in contrast*, and cite specific details."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Model frame: Both Homer's poem and Riordan's Chapter 15 explore the theme of ___. In Homer's version, ___, which creates a ___ tone. In contrast, Riordan ___, which makes the gods seem ___. This comparison shows that ___."},{"type":"directions","text":"Use your chart and Venn diagram to write a paragraph (4–6 sentences) answering: How does Riordan's retelling change the way we view the gods' jealousy and betrayal compared to the older poetic telling? Include one quote or detail from each text and at least two vocabulary words from today."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do both versions suggest about the gods?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both show that the gods are jealous and can trick and betray each other, so they are not perfect. Homer tells it formally, so the betrayal feels like a serious story being sung. Riordan uses humor and modern talk, so the gods seem more like silly, temperamental people."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the difference in tone change how you feel about the gods?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In Homer I see the gods as powerful but also gossiping about each other. In Riordan I laugh at them, so I take them less seriously and feel more like they are just like us."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.9"],"stem":"Which statement best compares Riordan's version with the Homeric excerpt?","choices":[{"text":"Both explore jealousy, betrayal, and trickery among the gods, but Riordan uses a humorous, modern voice while Homer's is formal and poetic.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. This names a shared theme and a clear difference in voice and tone."},{"text":"Riordan's chapter has a completely different theme because it is funny.","correct":false,"rationale":"Humor changes tone, not the theme; the jealousy and betrayal remain."},{"text":"Homer's poem is funnier than Riordan's chapter because it has more detail.","correct":false,"rationale":"This reverses the tones. Homer is formal; Riordan is humorous."},{"type":"x","text":"Both versions are told by Percy in the first person.","correct":false,"rationale":"Only Riordan's novel is narrated by Percy. Homer's is a singer's poetic telling."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing a comparison using precise vocabulary, transitions, and expanded noun phrases.","sayAsk":"Say: Rehearse your idea aloud first. Frames: Both texts show ___. However, Homer ___ while Riordan ___. The gods seem more ___ because ___. Encourage expanded noun phrases, such as the formal, poetic voice or the temperamental, jealous god.","watchFor":"If students write two summaries with no comparison, then prompt: What is the same? What is different? If students use I think, then prompt: Replace with The text shows. Success: students use a transition and include evidence from both texts."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: comparing two texts in writing","tryThis":"Provide the model frame and a completed Venn diagram row. Have students say each sentence to a partner before writing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: cross-text comparison","tryThis":"Ask students to add a sentence explaining why Riordan might retell the myth with humor for modern readers and what that suggests about how myths change over time."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students will reflect on what comparing two versions of a myth reveals and connect it to the performance task.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-exit","title":"Exit Ticket: What Changes, What Stays","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9","L.6.6"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In the performance task you will compare themes across versions of a mythic relationship. Today you practiced that by comparing Homer and Riordan."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the exit ticket: The theme that stays the same in both versions is ___. Riordan changes ___ by using ___, which makes the gods seem ___. One word from today that helped me describe this is ___ because ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The theme that stays the same in both versions is jealousy and betrayal. Riordan changes the tone by using humor and exaggeration, which makes the gods seem more like temperamental people. One word that helped me is gossip because it shows how the gods talk about each other's mistakes."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (optional)","purpose":"Students continue reading and prepare for the next lesson.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-ch15-16","title":"Read and Annotate","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.10"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Read and annotate The Lightning Thief Chapter 15, pp. 234–241.
